theme: Praise the LORD from the heavens
readingInstruction: Read Psalm 148. This psalm calls the whole creation to praise, from the angels to the sea monsters to kings and children. Notice the two halves: praise from the heavens (vv. 1-6) and praise from the earth (vv. 7-14).
settingTheScene: Psalm 148 is one of the Hallel psalms at the end of the Psalter (146 to 150). It is a hymn calling all of creation to praise the LORD. It has no named author, and it does not tell a story but sings an invitation. It prepares us for the last two weeks of Revelation, where every creature in heaven and on earth and under the earth and in the sea joins in worship (5:13). Today we will see the whole creation as a choir, with Christ as the horn that God has raised up.
observation: “Praise the LORD! Praise the LORD from the heavens; praise him in the heights!” (v. 1).
“Praise him, all his angels; praise him, all his hosts!” (v. 2).
“Praise him, sun and moon, praise him, all you shining stars!” (v. 3).
“Let them praise the name of the LORD! For he commanded and they were created” (v. 5).
“Praise the LORD from the earth, you great sea creatures and all deeps” (v. 7).
“Kings of the earth and all peoples, princes and all rulers of the earth!” (v. 11).
“Let them praise the name of the LORD, for his name alone is exalted” (v. 13).
“He has raised up a horn for his people, praise for all his saints” (v. 14).
interpretation:
The psalm starts above: “Praise the LORD from the heavens; praise him in the heights!” The angels and hosts, the sun and moon and stars, the highest heavens and the waters above the heavens are told to praise. The reason is given: “Let them praise the name of the LORD! For he commanded and they were created. And he established them forever and ever; he gave a decree, and it shall not pass away.” Creation praises by being what God made it to be, obeying his command. The heavens do not need words to praise him; their ordered existence proclaims his wisdom.

The second half comes down to the earth. “Praise the LORD from the earth, you great sea creatures and all deeps, fire and hail, snow and mist, stormy wind fulfilling his word! Mountains and all hills, fruit trees and all cedars! Beasts and all livestock, creeping things and flying birds!” The psalmist lists everything: sea monsters (which in other cultures were symbols of chaos and are here put in their place), weather, mountains, trees, animals. Then humanity: “Kings of the earth and all peoples, princes and all rulers of the earth! Young men and maidens together, old men and children!” The call goes from rulers to children, with no one left out. It includes every age and every rank.

The reason for human praise is the same: “Let them praise the name of the LORD, for his name alone is exalted; his majesty is above earth and heaven.” And then the psalm gives a particular reason for the people of God to praise: “He has raised up a horn for his people, praise for all his saints, for the people of Israel who are near to him.” A horn is a symbol of strength and, in this context, a ruler or savior from the house of David. Zechariah, in Luke 1:69, uses the same image for Jesus: “He has raised up a horn of salvation for us in the house of his servant David.” The creation praises its Maker, and the church praises the one who has saved it.

This psalm gives dignity to everything in creation, a reminder that the world is a stage for God’s glory. It also shows that our praise is part of something bigger. When we sing, we join the sun, the stars, the sea creatures, the trees, and the angels. And in Revelation 5:13, John hears “every creature in heaven and on earth and under the earth and in the sea, and all that is in them, saying, To him who sits on the throne and to the Lamb be blessing and honor and glory and might forever and ever!” Psalm 148 is the first draft of that chorus.
connection: Genesis 1 recounts the creation that Psalm 148 praises. Psalm 19:1-4 and 96:11-13 also have creation praising God. Isaiah 55:12 has trees clapping their hands. Job 38-41 shows the Creator’s care for the whole creation. Luke 1:69 uses the horn for Christ. Psalm 132:17 speaks of a horn for David. Romans 8:19-23 describes creation waiting for redemption. Colossians 1:16-20 describes all things created through and reconciled to Christ. Revelation 5:13 and 21:1-5 show all creation worshiping. Philippians 2:10-11 describes every knee bowing.
application:
Take a walk outside and notice one thing from each group in the psalm: the sky, the weather, a plant, an animal. Let each prompt a short prayer of praise.

Think about the whole range of ages and ranks in your church. Ask how you can include someone from a different age or background in worship.

Thank Christ for being the horn that God has raised up for his people.
prayerPrompts: Praise God from the heavens and from the earth.
Add your voice to the voices of angels and creation.
Tell him what in creation moves you to praise.
